newsitem.title: YEMEN: Freed German hostages in Yemen in good health.
newsitem.headline: Freed German hostages in Yemen in good health.

text.p: Seven German hostages released by their Yemeni kidnappers on Tuesday after a week in captivity are in good health and due to arrive in Sanaa from remote eastern Yemen later in the day, a German embassy spokesman said.
"They are in good health," he told Reuters.
The seven men, aged between 30 and 45, were to board a plane in the province of Hadramaut, 770 km (480 miles) to the east.
They were kidnapped by local tribesmen last week while riding motorcycles through the Wadi al-Dabaat area between Mahra and Hadramaut.
A security official said earlier the kidnappers agreed to release the Germans after security forces and troops tightened a siege on them.

He said last-minute negotiations had centred on the tribesmen's demand of a government amnesty in return for releasing their hostages. The official refused to say whether any of the demands had been met.
The German ambassador expressed gratitude for the safe release of the seven tourists and hoped it would be the last kidnapping in Yemen, the official Yemeni news agency SABA said.
Kidnapping is a common ploy by tribesmen holding grievances against the government or foreign oil firms operating in Yemen, one of the Arab world's most impoverished countries.

Scores of tourists, diplomats and other foreigners have been seized in recent years. They have tried to use the foreigners, who have included a U.S. diplomat and a Saudi ambassador, as bargaining chips.
Siege by security forces has been the usual government response.
In the latest incident, the tribesmen wanted to pressure the government to bring to justice an alleged Yemeni swindler who sold them cars smuggled from Gulf Arab states.
Security sources said the abductors originally telephoned local authorities to demand 12 million marks ($7 million) ransom to release the tourists, but police in Hadramaut denied that.
No casualties from past abductions have been reported and all the hostages have been released unharmed.
Some were rescued by security forces, others were set free.
In February, U.S. oil engineer Joe Dell'Aria was seized by members of the Murad tribe angered by a dispute over a piece of land in the capital. He was eventually released unharmed.
Five Polish tourists held for eight days by another tribe in December were kept captive to demand compensation for damage sustained during flooding.
"They did not want to harm us," one of the Poles said on return to Warsaw.

Earlier in December two groups of Dutch tourists were kidnapped in separate incidents. In one, north of Sanaa, three Yemeni soldiers were killed and five wounded when the kidnappers fired rocket-propelled grenades at surrounding military forces.
